chapters.title: Introduction and Overview of Requirements Engineering

questions.prompt: A requirements document for a mobile banking app contains the statement: "The app shall be able to process at least 10,000 transactions per minute during peak hours." How should this statement be classified?

options.text: A quality requirement, because it concerns a performance/capacity concern not covered by the system's functional behavior
A constraint, because it restricts the solution space beyond what is necessary for the functional requirements
A functional requirement, because it describes a result the system must provide
Both a functional and a quality requirement at the same time, since it specifies a numeric behavior

questions.explanation: Quality requirements cover quality concerns not addressed by functional requirements, such as performance. The popular heuristic "what the system shall do = functional, how = quality" is misleading here: statements about data volume or processing speed are quality requirements, not functional ones, even though they look like capability statements (EU 1.1 Requirements Engineering: What).

questions.prompt: According to the CPRE glossary definition underlying this syllabus, the term "requirement" denotes three distinct concepts simultaneously. Which option correctly lists these three concepts?

options.text: A system requirement; a stakeholder requirement; a user requirement
A need perceived by a stakeholder; a capability or property that a system shall have; a documented representation of a need, capability, or property
A problem; a requirement; a solution
An elicited requirement; a validated requirement; a managed requirement
A functional requirement; a quality requirement; a constraint

questions.explanation: The term "requirement" is defined to cover a perceived need, a required capability/property, and its documented representation — three facets of one concept. Option E lists kinds of requirements by content, A lists perspective-based forms of requirements, and C describes the problem-requirement-solution relationship; D lists lifecycle activities. These are different classifications from the glossary's three meanings.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is NOT listed in the syllabus as a typical cause contributing to missing, unclear, or incorrect requirements?

options.text: The assumption that the requirements are self-evident
Excessive stakeholder involvement early in the project
Rushing straight into building the system

questions.explanation: The syllabus names rushing into implementation, communication problems, the false assumption that requirements are self-evident, and inadequate RE education/skills as causes of inadequate RE. Involving stakeholders early and broadly is encouraged (see EU2 Principle 2), not a cause of poor RE; therefore B is the odd one out.

questions.prompt: The syllabus distinguishes between *forms of occurrence* of requirements (e.g., system requirements, domain requirements) and *kinds of requirements classified by content* (functional, quality, constraint). Which TWO of the following terms belong to the "forms of occurrence" perspective rather than the "kind of requirement" perspective?
questions.explanation: System requirements and domain requirements describe *where/how* a requirement occurs (perspective-based), alongside stakeholder, user, and business requirements. Functional requirements, quality requirements, and constraints instead classify requirements by their *content* — a different, orthogonal distinction made in EU1.1.

questions.prompt: Which TWO of the following are explicitly named in the syllabus as typical CAUSES of missing, unclear, or incorrect requirements — as distinct from being symptoms of inadequate RE themselves?

options.text: Rushing straight into building the system

questions.explanation: Rushing into implementation and communication problems between involved parties are named causes of inadequate RE. Missing, unclear, and incorrect requirements (A, B, and D) are the *symptoms* of inadequate RE, not its causes, and using agile processes (C) is not mentioned as a cause at all.

questions.prompt: ProjectCo's corporate IT policy mandates that any new internal system must be built on the company's existing Java-based microservices platform, regardless of which technology would otherwise be best suited for the task. How should this statement be classified?

options.text: Constraint — it restricts the solution space (choice of technology) beyond what is necessary to meet the functional and quality requirements
Functional requirement — it describes what the system shall do
Stakeholder requirement — it only reflects the IT department's perspective

questions.explanation: Constraints limit the solution space beyond what is needed to satisfy functional and quality requirements. Mandating a specific technology platform regardless of suitability is a classic constraint, not a description of system behavior (functional) or of a quality attribute like maintainability.

questions.prompt: Consider the following statements about the different forms in which requirements can occur, as distinguished in the syllabus. For each, decide whether it is True or False.

statements.text: System requirements describe what a system shall do, as observed at the interface between the system and its environment.
Stakeholder requirements and user requirements are identical terms describing exactly the same group of people.
Domain requirements specify required domain properties that are relevant to understanding the system.
Business requirements describe the detailed user-interface design of a system.
User requirements express the desires and needs of a system's users from their own perspective.

questions.explanation: (1) True — this matches the definition of system requirements. (2) False — user requirements are a subset of stakeholder requirements, not identical to them. (3) True — domain requirements capture required domain properties. (4) False — business requirements concern business goals, objectives, and needs, not UI design. (5) True — this matches the definition of user requirements.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each of the following statements about Requirements Engineering tasks and the role of a Requirements Engineer is True or False.

statements.text: Requirements analysis and conflict resolution are considered part of elicitation rather than separate top-level RE tasks.
"Requirements Engineer" is typically a distinct job title listed in most companies' organizational charts.
Every RE endeavor requires an RE process tailored from a broad range of possibilities; there is no single standard process.
Only people holding the official title "Requirements Engineer" are capable of performing elicitation, documentation, validation, or management of requirements.

questions.explanation: (1) True — the syllabus states analysis and conflict resolution are part of elicitation. (2) False — Requirements Engineer is typically a role, not a job title; business analysts, product owners, systems engineers, and developers commonly act in this role. (3) True — a suitable RE process must be tailored for every endeavor. (4) False — this contradicts (2); many job functions act in the Requirements Engineer role.
questions.reference: EU1.4 / EU1.5 — Requirements Engineering: How / The Role and Tasks of a Requirements Engineer

questions.prompt: A small internal tool used by three back-office staff, with negligible risk if a minor UI quirk occurs, is nonetheless specified by the RE team with an exhaustive 40-page formal specification, including pixel-level layout rules, consuming three weeks of elicitation and review effort. Which principle is most clearly violated by the Requirements Engineers' approach?

options.text: Stakeholders — too few stakeholders were consulted
Value-orientation — the cost of this extensive specification effort likely exceeds its benefit given the low risk and criticality of the system
Validation — the requirements were never validated
Context — the system's context boundary was never defined
Innovation — the team failed to propose creative new features

questions.explanation: The value of a requirement is its benefit minus its cost, and the effort invested in RE should be proportional to risk and criticality. Spending three weeks on an exhaustive, pixel-level specification for a low-risk, low-criticality internal tool is disproportionate to the benefit gained, violating value-orientation. Nothing in the scenario indicates problems with stakeholder coverage, validation, innovation, or context.

questions.prompt: A Requirements Engineer elicited requirements by interviewing only the system's end users and the marketing department that commissioned the project. Shortly after go-live, the system failed a mandatory compliance audit because the data-retention and access-logging needs of the corporate compliance officer were never captured. Which principle was violated?

options.text: Evolution — the requirements were not permitted to change after go-live
Value-orientation — too much effort was spent eliciting requirements
Problem–Requirement–Solution — a solution was designed before any problem existed
Stakeholders — not all relevant stakeholder roles were identified and consulted, so critical requirements from the compliance officer (a regulator-like role) were missed

questions.explanation: It is not sufficient to consider only the requirements of end users and customers; doing so risks missing critical requirements from other stakeholder roles, such as a compliance officer or regulator. The failure here is a direct consequence of incomplete stakeholder identification, not of excessive RE effort, requirement freezing, or solution-first thinking.

questions.prompt: During a workshop, a client and the development team both nodded in agreement when discussing a requirement labeled "fast checkout process." Weeks later, the developers delivered a checkout flow optimized for a minimal number of clicks, while the client had envisioned a flow optimized for minimal page-load time. Nobody had checked beforehand whether both parties interpreted "fast" the same way. Which concept from Principle 3 best explains this situation?

options.text: A false shared understanding existed — both parties believed they agreed, but in fact interpreted the requirement differently
An obstacle to shared understanding, namely high team turnover, caused the misunderstanding
The requirement was actually a constraint rather than a functional requirement, which caused the confusion
A true explicit shared understanding was achieved, but the requirement was poorly documented afterward

questions.explanation: Both implicit and explicit shared understanding may be false: people can believe they share an understanding while actually interpreting it differently. Nodding in agreement without validating the shared meaning of "fast" is exactly this trap; nothing indicates team turnover was the cause, and the classification as constraint vs. functional requirement is unrelated to the misunderstanding.

questions.prompt: An automated parking-gate requirement states: "The gate control system shall only lift the barrier when a valid ticket has been detected." Satisfying this requirement depends on the ticket reader hardware correctly detecting ticket barcodes under all on-site lighting conditions. What does this dependency represent, according to Principle 4 (Context)?

options.text: A quality requirement concerning the reliability of the gate control system
A constraint that limits the solution space of the gate control system
A functional requirement for the gate control system itself
An assumption about a real-world phenomenon in the system's context that must hold for the system requirement to be meaningfully satisfiable

questions.explanation: Domain assumptions are assumptions about real-world phenomena in a system's context that must hold for the system to work and its requirements to be met — analogous to the radar/air-traffic-control example in the handbook. The barcode reading correctly under all lighting is outside the gate controller's own requirements; it is a context assumption, not itself a functional, quality, or constraint requirement on the controller.

questions.prompt: Which of the following statements about Principle 5 (Problem – Requirement – Solution) is CORRECT?

options.text: Although problems, requirements, and solutions are inevitably intertwined in practice, Requirements Engineers still strive to separate these concerns as far as possible when thinking, communicating, and documenting
Because the three are inevitably intertwined, Requirements Engineers should abandon any attempt to separate them when documenting
Solution ideas can never give rise to new requirements — only existing problems can do so
Problems, requirements, and solutions always occur strictly in this order: first the problem, then the requirement, then the solution

questions.explanation: The syllabus explicitly states that despite their intertwinement, Requirements Engineers aim to separate problem, requirement, and solution concerns as far as possible for the sake of manageability. Option D is wrong because innovative systems may start from a solution idea instead; B contradicts the separation-of-concerns guidance; D is wrong because solution ideas can create new user needs that become requirements.

questions.prompt: A quality assurance team checks that a delivered module strictly conforms to its written specification document. A Requirements Engineer instead checks, together with stakeholders, whether the specified requirements actually reflect what the stakeholders need. Which of these two activities corresponds to "validation" as defined under Principle 6?

options.text: The quality assurance team's check, because it confirms conformance to a specification
The Requirements Engineer's check, because validation confirms that an item matches the stakeholders' needs
Neither activity represents validation; validation can only be performed after the system is deployed

questions.explanation: Validation is defined as confirming that an item matches the stakeholders' needs — this is what the Requirements Engineer did. Checking conformance to a written specification is a verification-style activity, not validation. Validation must start already during RE, not only after deployment, which rules out D.

questions.prompt: A Scrum team argues: "We are agile, so we don't need any systematic process or discipline for handling requirements — we just talk to the product owner whenever needed." How does Principle 9 (Systematic and disciplined work) address this argument?

options.text: Only plan-driven, waterfall-style projects require systematic RE; agile projects are exempt by definition
The team is correct: agile processes are explicitly exempt from needing systematic RE practices
Agility and flexibility are not valid excuses for unsystematic, ad hoc work; even agile teams must employ RE practices suited to their context
Systematic and disciplined work means always reusing the exact same RE process regardless of context

questions.explanation: The syllabus/handbook explicitly states that agility and flexibility are not valid excuses for an unsystematic, ad hoc style of work in RE. At the same time, systematic work does not mean reusing the same process every time — there is no "one size fits all," which rules out C, and Principle 9 applies regardless of the chosen development process, ruling out A and D.
questions.reference: EU2.2 — Principle 9: Systematic and disciplined work

questions.prompt: Name the TWO forms of shared understanding distinguished under Principle 3.
questions.explanation: The syllabus distinguishes explicit shared understanding (achieved through documented and agreed requirements) and implicit shared understanding (based on shared knowledge about needs, visions, and context). "Formal," "partial," and "verified" shared understanding are not terms used in the syllabus or handbook.

questions.prompt: Name the THREE reasons explicitly listed in the syllabus as typical causes of requests to change a requirement (Principle 7 – Evolution).

options.text: Clients changing their priorities or opinions
Mandatory annual security audits of the RE process
Developers requesting a cleaner code architecture
Competitors launching new products or services
A decrease in the overall team size
A Requirements Engineer being promoted to a management position

questions.explanation: The syllabus lists changed business processes, competitors launching new products or services, and clients changing their priorities or opinions among the typical causes of requirement change (alongside changes in technology, changes of laws/regulations, and user feedback, not listed here). Options D, E, F, and G are plausible-sounding but are not among the causes named in the syllabus.

questions.prompt: According to Principle 8 (Innovation), on which TWO scales does RE shape innovative systems?

options.text: Large scale — striving for disruptive new ideas
Enterprise scale — standardizing cross-department business processes
Small scale — striving for exciting new features and ease of use
Medium scale — improving internal code quality

questions.explanation: The syllabus states RE shapes innovative systems on a small scale by striving for exciting new features and ease of use, and on a large scale by striving for disruptive new ideas. Code quality, business-process standardization, and database schema optimization are technical/architectural concerns not framed as RE's innovation scales.

questions.prompt: For each of the following factors, decide whether it is listed as an ENABLER of shared understanding (True) or as an OBSTACLE to shared understanding (False), per Principle 3.

statements.text: Domain knowledge shared among the people involved.
Outsourcing part of the development work to a third party.
Previous successful collaboration between stakeholders and developers.
High turnover among the people involved in the project.
Large geographic distance between team members.

questions.explanation: (1) True — domain knowledge is listed as an enabler. (2) False — outsourcing is listed as an obstacle. (3) True — previous successful collaboration is an enabler. (4) False — high turnover is an obstacle. (5) False — geographic distance is an obstacle.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each of the following statements about the nine principles of Requirements Engineering is True or False.

statements.text: According to Principle 1 (Value-orientation), the value of a requirement is defined as its benefit minus its cost.
According to Principle 4 (Context), the system boundary and the scope of a system development always coincide exactly, with no exceptions.
According to Principle 6 (Validation), validating requirements should only begin once the system has been fully implemented and deployed.
According to Principle 9 (Systematic and disciplined work), there is no single RE process or practice that works well in every situation.

questions.explanation: (1) True — this is the explicit definition of a requirement's value. (2) False — the system boundary and scope do not always coincide; some in-boundary elements are out of scope (reused as-is) and some context elements are in scope. (3) False — validation must start already during RE, not only after deployment. (4) True — there is no "one size fits all" RE process or practice.

chapters.title: Work Products Overview, Natural-Language-Based & Template-Based Work Products / Model-Based Work Products, Glossaries, Documentation Structures, Prototypes & Quality Criteria

questions.prompt:
During a design workshop for CityFlex, the RE team draws a quick whiteboard sketch showing how a driver unlocks a car via the app; the sketch is only meant to support the discussion in the room. Separately, they maintain a continuously growing list of user stories in the product backlog, which already has an assigned owner, a status, and a revision history. Finally, the "CityFlex System Requirements Specification v1.0" has just been formally signed off by the product owner and is now subject to strict change control.

According to the three lifespan categories of work products, how should these three work products be classified?

options.text: Sketch = evolving; user story list = durable; specification = temporary
Sketch = temporary; user story list = evolving; specification = durable
All three are evolving work products, since they all document requirements in some form.
Sketch = temporary; user story list = durable; specification = evolving
Sketch = durable; user story list = evolving; specification = temporary

questions.explanation: Temporary work products support communication and shared understanding and are typically discarded without metadata (the whiteboard sketch); evolving work products emerge iteratively and should carry at least owner, status, and revision-history metadata (the growing backlog); durable work products have been baselined or released and require a full set of metadata plus change control (the signed-off specification). Option C ignores that lifespan status depends on baselining/release, not merely on documenting requirements.

questions.prompt:
In the draft CityFlex system requirements specification, one paragraph states: "REQ-12: The app shall reduce the average time users spend searching for an available car by promoting a better overall mobility experience in the city." The very next paragraph states: "REQ-13: When the user taps the 'Unlock' button on the car details screen, the app shall send an unlock command to the vehicle's onboard unit within 2 seconds."

What problem does this excerpt illustrate?

options.text: REQ-13 is an unwanted-behavior requirement and must never appear directly after a functional requirement.
The excerpt is unproblematic, since large specifications may freely interleave abstraction levels as long as requirements are numbered.
REQ-12 violates the rule that quality requirements must always be stated quantitatively.
REQ-12 and REQ-13 mix two different abstraction levels within the same section, which the syllabus advises against.
REQ-12 is a constraint and therefore must appear only in a dedicated "Constraints" chapter.

questions.explanation: REQ-12 is a vague, high-level vision/goal-level statement, while REQ-13 is a detailed, system-level requirement; the syllabus states that requirements at different abstraction levels should not be mixed, and in large documents they must be kept separate through appropriate structuring. There is no rule against an unwanted-behavior-style requirement following a goal statement (B), and REQ-12 is not described as a constraint (E) nor is "must always be quantified" an actual rule (C).

questions.prompt:
CityFlex's RE team is deciding how detailed to specify the requirement for integrating the vehicle's onboard unlocking hardware. This work will be outsourced to an external supplier abroad who has never worked with CityFlex before, has little domain knowledge of car-sharing systems, and with whom rapid feedback cycles are not available.

Based on the factors influencing the level of detail (EU3.1.3), what should the RE team do?

options.text: Specify this requirement in considerable detail, because an unfamiliar supplier, low shared understanding, and the absence of rapid feedback all increase the need for detail.
Avoid specifying this requirement at all and let the supplier reverse-engineer it from a prototype.
Specify this requirement only qualitatively, because quality requirements never need to be detailed.
Specify this requirement at a relatively low level of detail, since outsourced work should always leave maximum design freedom.

questions.explanation: The syllabus names low familiarity with the project context, low shared understanding, and lack of rapid stakeholder feedback as factors that increase the necessary level of detail; all three apply here, so a detailed specification is warranted even though it costs more effort. Options B, C, and D ignore these risk factors.

questions.prompt:
Consider this excerpt describing a CityFlex interaction: "When a registered driver requests to reserve a car (context), the app checks the car's real-time availability and battery-level data (structure and data), changes the car's status to 'Reserved' (state transition), then verifies payment details and displays a confirmation screen to the driver (function and flow)."

Which aspect from "Aspects to be Considered in Work Products" is notably **NOT** addressed by this excerpt, even though it is also a necessary aspect to document?
questions.explanation: The excerpt explicitly covers context (the driver's request), structure and data (availability/battery data), state and behavior (status change to "Reserved"), and function and flow (payment check, confirmation display) — but it specifies no quality aspect, such as how quickly the confirmation must appear. Options A, C, D, and E are the aspects already addressed.
questions.reference: EU3.1.4 — Aspects to be Considered in Work Products

questions.prompt:
The CityFlex glossary defines "Reservation" as "a booking of a car for a specified time window." The system requirements specification, the use-case document, and the mobile app's UI-text specification each include an identical, word-for-word copy of this same definition instead of simply referencing the glossary entry.

Which general documentation guideline is being violated here?

options.text: Use terms consistently, as defined in the glossary.
Select a work product type that fits the intended purpose.
Avoid redundancy by referencing content instead of repeating the same content again.

questions.explanation: Copying the identical definition verbatim into multiple documents instead of referencing the single glossary entry is exactly the redundancy the syllabus warns against; terminology itself stays consistent here (A), so the violated guideline is the no-redundancy rule, not the consistent-terminology rule.

questions.prompt: Name the three statements that correctly describe **evolving** work products, per EU3.1.1.

options.text: They have already been baselined or released.
They typically emerge through several iterations over time.
Depending on their importance and status, change control procedures may need to apply.
At least owner, status, and revision history should be kept as metadata.
They always require the identical full set of metadata that durable work products need.
They are discarded immediately after use, and no metadata is kept about them.

questions.explanation: Evolving work products (e.g., a growing collection of user stories) emerge iteratively, need at least basic metadata (owner, status, revision history), and may require change control depending on importance/status. Option A describes durable work products, E overstates their metadata requirement (the full set applies to durable work products), and F describes temporary work products.

questions.prompt: Per the overview of frequently used work products (EU3.1.1), which three of the following are classified as work products for a **coherent set of requirements**, as opposed to a single-requirement or document-level work product?
questions.explanation: Use cases, graphic models, and epics (along with task descriptions and external interface descriptions) represent coherent sets of requirements. Individual requirements and user stories (B, D) are single-requirement work products, the system requirements specification (E) is a comprehensive document, and the glossary (F) falls under "other work products."

questions.prompt: The CityFlex project lead claims several benefits for defining the set of work products to be used early in the project. Which **three** of the following claims are **NOT** actually among the benefits described in EU3.1.6 (i.e., they are false or unsupported)?

options.text: It ensures that appropriate notations are used.
It avoids redundancy, resulting in less work and easier maintainability.
It guarantees that stakeholders will never change their requirements again.
It helps in planning efforts and resources.
It removes the need to keep any metadata on durable work products.
It eliminates the need to ever maintain a glossary.

questions.explanation: The syllabus lists planning efforts/resources, ensuring appropriate notations, ensuring results are recorded in the right work products, avoiding late "final editing," and avoiding redundancy as genuine benefits of early work-product planning — so A, C, and F are true. Claims B, D, and E are overclaims/false: early planning does not freeze stakeholder requirements, does not remove the need for a glossary, and does not remove the metadata obligations of durable work products.
questions.reference: EU3.1.6 — Plan the Work Products to be Used

questions.prompt: Judge the following statements about the characteristics of RE work products as true or false.

statements.text: Work products are characterized by their purpose, representation, size, and life span (and storage).
A temporary work product can later become an evolving work product by adding metadata and continuing to maintain it.
A work product may never contain another work product; each work product must stand entirely on its own.
Durable work products require only minimal metadata, since they are already considered "finished."
Informal, temporary work products — such as sticky notes on a Kanban board — may be stored on non-electronic media.

questions.explanation: (1) Matches the facets listed in the syllabus. (2) Matches the described transition from temporary to evolving work products. (3) False — the syllabus explicitly notes a work product may contain other work products. (4) False — durable work products need a full set of metadata and an elaborate change process. (5) True — explicitly mentioned as an example of non-electronic storage.

questions.prompt: The CityFlex team is reviewing how they document different aspects of requirements. Judge each statement as true or false, per EU3.1.4.

statements.text: A requirement about the data structure of a "Car" entity (e.g., its license plate, battery level, and status fields) falls under the "structure and data" aspect.
A requirement describing how the app's screen changes when a car transitions from "Available" to "Reserved" falls under the "function and flow" aspect.
Stakeholders tend to take quality requirements for granted and consequently often omit them when specifying requirements.
Constraints should generally be documented as if they were functional requirements, since both describe what the system must do.
The "context and boundary" aspect covers external actors and the interfaces between the system and its environment.

questions.explanation: (1) Correct categorization. (2) False — a state transition of the system belongs to "state and behavior," not "function and flow." (3) Matches the syllabus observation about stakeholders omitting quality requirements. (4) False — the syllabus flags mislabeling constraints as functional requirements as a common mistake Requirements Engineers must avoid. (5) Correct categorization.
questions.reference: EU3.1.4 — Aspects to be Considered in Work Products

questions.prompt: Which of the following statements about natural-language-based work products is **INCORRECT**, according to EU3.2?

options.text: Texts written in natural language can frequently be interpreted in more than one way.
No specific training is required to read and understand natural-language texts, since natural language is used in everyday life and taught at school.
Natural language is extremely expressive and flexible, so almost any conceivable requirement can be expressed in it.
Using natural language for requirements automatically eliminates the risk of differing interpretations by different readers.
Detecting ambiguities, omissions, and inconsistencies in natural-language texts is difficult and expensive.

questions.explanation: The syllabus explicitly states that natural-language texts can "frequently be interpreted in different ways," which is precisely the problem that detection of ambiguities, omissions, and inconsistencies is difficult and expensive to address — so D's claim of "automatically eliminating" misinterpretation risk directly contradicts the syllabus, while A, B, C, and E are all stated advantages/disadvantages.

questions.prompt:
In the CityFlex draft specification, REQ-21 reads: "The reservation shall be cancelled automatically if payment fails."

Which pitfall of natural-language-based requirements does REQ-21 risk, and why?

options.text: Unspecific noun — because "payment" can never be used as a noun in a requirement.
Universal quantifier — because "automatically" is a universal quantifier like "all" or "never."
Incomplete comparison — because "automatically" has no stated reference object.
Passive voice — because the requirement does not state which component or actor is responsible for cancelling the reservation.

questions.explanation: "Shall be cancelled" is phrased in the passive voice with no explicit acting subject, which can hide which part of the system is responsible for the cancellation — exactly the passive-voice pitfall described in EU3.2. There is no comparison being made (C) and "automatically" is neither a universal quantifier (B) nor does "payment" itself make the sentence an unspecific-noun problem (C).
questions.reference: EU3.2 — Natural-Language-Based Work Products (Pitfalls of Technical Writing)

questions.prompt:
REQ-22 states: "The CityFlex app shall always display the nearest available car first."

What should the RE team specifically check before accepting this requirement as written, per the guidance on universal quantifiers?

options.text: Whether "nearest" is measured on a ratio scale.
Whether the requirement should be rewritten in passive voice to hide responsibility.
Whether "always" really denotes a universal rule with no exceptions, or whether exceptional cases exist that must be specified separately.
Whether the sentence correctly uses the auxiliary verb "shall" rather than "should."

questions.explanation: The syllabus/handbook advise that whenever a universal quantifier such as "always" or "never" is used, the author must reflect on whether the property is truly universal or whether it is a general rule with unstated exceptions that also need to be specified. Options B–D address unrelated concerns (measurement scales, modal-verb conventions, and passive voice).
questions.reference: EU3.2 — Natural-Language-Based Work Products (Pitfalls of Technical Writing)

questions.prompt:
REQ-23 states: "Only after successful verification, the driver shall be allowed to start the trip."

Per the guidance on nominalizations, what must the RE team additionally check?

options.text: Whether the sentence should be rewritten using the EARS "WHILE" template.
Whether "verification" should instead be replaced by a universal quantifier.
Whether "verification" is spelled consistently with the glossary term "authentication."
Whether there is a complementary requirement (or set of requirements) that actually specifies the verification procedure itself.

questions.explanation: "Verification" is a nominalization (a noun derived from a verb) that, like the syllabus's "authentication" example, may hide an unspecified procedure; the Requirements Engineer must check whether requirements describing that underlying procedure actually exist elsewhere. Options A, B, and C address unrelated concerns.
questions.reference: EU3.2 — Natural-Language-Based Work Products (Pitfalls of Technical Writing)

questions.prompt:
Review REQ-24 from the CityFlex draft: "If the car is returned after the scheduled time, a fee may apply to the user."

Name the **two** pitfalls from EU3.2 that this requirement exhibits.

options.text: Passive voice hides all responsibility in the sentence, since no verb at all is used.
Unspecific nouns — "the user" and "a fee" are left vague instead of referring to precisely defined terms or values.
Universal quantifier — "scheduled" is used as a universal quantifier such as "always" or "never."
Incomplete condition — it states no threshold for how late the car must be, and no explicit case for an on-time return.
Incomplete comparison — "scheduled time" is used as a comparative with no reference object at all.
Nominalization — "car" is a noun derived from a verb.

questions.explanation: The requirement gives no concrete lateness threshold and no else-case for an on-time return (incomplete condition), and leaves "the user" and "a fee" unspecific instead of precise values or identifiers (unspecific nouns). There is an explicit reference object ("the scheduled time"), so E is wrong; the sentence uses passive voice (A), not active voice; "car" is not a nominalization (F); and "scheduled" is not a universal quantifier (C).
questions.reference: EU3.2 — Natural-Language-Based Work Products (Pitfalls of Technical Writing)

questions.prompt: Which **three** of the following are recommended rules for writing good natural-language-based requirements, per EU3.2?

options.text: Write short, well-structured sentences, ideally one requirement per sentence.
Maximize the use of nominalizations to keep sentences short.
Define and consistently use a uniform terminology via a glossary.
Avoid vague or ambiguous terms and phrases.
Prefer passive voice throughout to sound more objective and formal.
Use universal quantifiers such as "always" and "never" as often as possible to be maximally strict.

questions.explanation: The syllabus lists writing short, well-structured sentences, defining and consistently using uniform terminology, and avoiding vague or ambiguous terms/phrases as rules supporting good natural-language requirements. Passive voice (E) and universal quantifiers (F) are things to use only "with care," not to maximize, and nominalizations (B) are a pitfall to handle carefully, not a technique to maximize.

questions.prompt: For each CityFlex requirement excerpt or claim below, judge whether the statement is TRUE or FALSE, per EU3.2.

statements.text: "The battery level shall be checked regularly." — This exhibits an incomplete-description-style problem because "regularly" and "the battery level" leave the frequency and exact subject underspecified.
"The system shall never allow two users to reserve the same car simultaneously." — Using the universal quantifier "never" here is automatically wrong and must always be removed from any requirement.
"The app is faster than the previous CityFlex release." — This is a complete comparison, because it names a reference object ("the previous release").
Passive voice is strictly forbidden in RE natural-language requirements and must never be used under any circumstances.
A nominalization such as "cancellation" in a requirement may hide an unspecified procedure that itself needs separate requirements.

questions.explanation: (1) Vague frequency/subject is a genuine issue. (2) False — universal quantifiers must be used "with care" and reflected upon, not automatically banned; here it may well state a genuinely universal property. (3) True — a reference object is given. (4) False — passive voice is to be used "with care," not strictly forbidden. (5) True — matches the "authentication" example pattern.
questions.reference: EU3.2 — Natural-Language-Based Work Products (Pitfalls of Technical Writing)

questions.prompt:
"WHEN a registered driver taps 'Reserve' on an available car's details screen, the CityFlex app shall lock that car for the driver for 15 minutes."

Which EARS phrase-template category does this requirement instance belong to?
questions.explanation: The "WHEN <trigger> the <system name> shall <system response>" structure is the EARS template for event-driven requirements, triggered by an external event (the driver's tap). It is not an always-true ubiquitous rule (A), an undesired-situation template (C), a state-based "WHILE" rule (D), or a feature-conditional "WHERE" rule (E).
questions.reference: EU3.3 — Template-Based Work Products (Phrase Templates — EARS)

questions.prompt:
"WHILE a car is in 'Maintenance' state, the CityFlex app shall prevent any driver from reserving that car."

Which EARS phrase-template category does this requirement belong to?
questions.explanation: The "WHILE <in a specific state> the <system name> shall <system response>" structure is the EARS template for state-driven requirements that apply only in a certain state — here, the car's "Maintenance" state. It is not triggered by a discrete event (E) nor is it about an undesired situation (C) or an optional feature (E).
questions.reference: EU3.3 — Template-Based Work Products (Phrase Templates — EARS)

questions.prompt:
"IF a trip is in progress and the car's battery drops below 5%, THEN the CityFlex app shall notify the driver to return the car immediately."

Which EARS category does this requirement belong to, and why does EARS treat this as a category distinct from event-driven requirements?

options.text: Unwanted behavior, because it addresses an undesired/exceptional situation — a frequent source of omissions that EARS deliberately separates from ordinary event-driven requirements.
Event-driven, because WHEN and IF/THEN have exactly identical semantics in EARS.
State-driven, because "in progress" exclusively describes a system state.
Optional feature, because the battery sensor is an optional component.
Ubiquitous, because the requirement must always hold regardless of state.

questions.explanation: The "IF <optional preconditions> <trigger>, THEN the <system name> shall <system response>" template captures unwanted behavior; although structurally similar to the event-driven template, EARS keeps it separate because unwanted/unexpected situations (failures, attacks, edge cases) are a major source of requirements omissions. It is not merely an ordinary event-driven rule (B), not a rule that must always hold (C), and not about an optional feature (D); "in progress" alone does not make this primarily state-driven (E).
questions.reference: EU3.3 — Template-Based Work Products (Phrase Templates — EARS)

questions.prompt:
A CityFlex user story reads: "As a driver, I want to filter the car list by vehicle type."

Per Cohn's phrase template and current best practice for user stories, what is missing, and why is it a problem?

options.text: The story illegally mixes a user story with a use-case form template.
The `<benefit>` clause is missing; although Cohn originally treated it as optional, current best practice is to always specify a benefit so the story's value is clear.
The `<role>` placeholder is missing, making it impossible to tell who wants the function.
An acceptance criterion is embedded directly in the sentence, which violates the phrase template.

questions.explanation: Cohn's template is "As a `<role>` I want `<requirement>` so that `<benefit>`"; the story has a role and a requirement but no "so that..." benefit clause. The syllabus/handbook note that, while Cohn originally made the benefit optional, standard practice today is to always include it. The role is present (contradicting A), no acceptance criterion or form-template mixing is present (C, D).
questions.reference: EU3.3 — Template-Based Work Products (Phrase Templates — User Stories)

questions.prompt:
The CityFlex team documents a use case titled "Reserve a Car" using a Cockburn-style form template, filling in Name, Precondition, Success end condition, Primary actor, Trigger, and Normal flow. They skip the "Alternate flows" and "Extensions" fields entirely, reasoning that "nothing unusual ever happens."

What risk does this illustrate, per EU3.3's discussion of template-based work products?

options.text: No risk — Alternate flows and Extensions are purely decorative fields that may always be omitted safely.
This violates the EARS unwanted-behavior rule, which the syllabus says applies only to model-based work products.

Aspects not included when filling in a template are more likely to be omitted altogether, so leaving these fields blank risks losing exception/alternative-handling requirements rather than merely reflecting their absence.
The use case must be rewritten entirely as a phrase template, since form templates cannot represent exceptions.

questions.explanation: A documented disadvantage of template-based work products is that aspects not covered by the template (or left blank within it) are more likely to be omitted from the requirements altogether — here, genuine exception-handling requirements may simply never get captured. A understates the real risk; C and D misstate how form templates and EARS relate to this situation.
questions.reference: EU3.3 — Template-Based Work Products (Form Templates; Advantages and Disadvantages)

questions.prompt:
Using a measurable-quality-requirement form template (with fields such as ID, Goal, Scale, Meter, Minimum, OK range, Desired), the CityFlex team writes: "Elapsed time in seconds (ratio scale), measured from the moment the driver taps 'Reserve' until the confirmation screen appears."

Which field(s) of the template does this text fill in?
questions.explanation: "Elapsed time in seconds (ratio scale)" states the measurement Scale, while "measured from the moment... until..." describes the measuring procedure, which is the Meter. It does not state a qualitative goal (A), nor any acceptable/minimum/desired value ranges (C, D, E).
questions.reference: EU3.3 — Template-Based Work Products (Form Templates — Measurable Quality Requirements)

questions.prompt: Which **three** of the following are **NOT** genuine advantages of template-based work products, per EU3.3 (i.e., they are overclaims not supported by the syllabus)?

options.text: They help capture the most relevant information, reducing errors of omission.
They provide a clear, re-usable structure.
They make requirements and specifications look uniform.
They eliminate the need for a glossary or shared terminology.
They automatically improve stakeholder communication without any training.
They guarantee that all requirements are complete and unambiguous.

questions.explanation: The syllabus credits templates with providing a clear, re-usable structure, helping capture relevant information, making work products look uniform, and improving overall quality (A, B, C are true). It does **not** claim templates guarantee completeness/unambiguity (D), eliminate the need for a glossary (E), or work "automatically" without training (E) — these are overclaims and are in fact contradicted by the documented pitfall that templates can lead to focusing on form over content.
questions.reference: EU3.3 — Template-Based Work Products (Advantages and Disadvantages)

questions.prompt: Name the **two** disadvantages/pitfalls of template-based work products described in EU3.3.

options.text: Templates eliminate the Requirements Engineer's need to understand the problem domain.
People often focus on formally completing the template rather than on the content.
Templates make work products look inconsistent across a project.
Aspects that are not included in the template are more likely to be omitted.
Templates cannot be customized for customer-specific needs.
Templates always increase the total page count of a specification beyond what is necessary.

questions.explanation: The syllabus names exactly two pitfalls of templates: a focus on formal completion over content, and the increased likelihood of omitting aspects not covered by the template. Templates are documented to make work products look more uniform, not inconsistent (C); customer-specific templates are explicitly mentioned as common practice (D is false); page count and domain knowledge are not addressed as pitfalls (E, F).
questions.reference: EU3.3 — Template-Based Work Products (Advantages and Disadvantages)

questions.prompt: Judge whether each example below is correctly matched to its template category (phrase, form, or document template), per EU3.3.

statements.text: "WHEN `<optional preconditions>` `<trigger>` the `<system name>` shall `<system response>`" (EARS) is an example of a phrase template.
"As a `<role>` I want `<requirement>` so that `<benefit>`" (Cohn) is an example of a form template.
Cockburn's structure with fields such as Name, Precondition, Normal flow, and Alternate flows for use cases is an example of a form template.
A structure such as "Part I Introduction / Part II System overview / Part III System requirements" for a whole system requirements specification is an example of a document template.

The measurable-quality-requirement template with fields ID, Goal, Scale, Meter, Minimum, OK range, Desired is a phrase template, since it is used to specify quality requirements rather than functional ones.

questions.explanation: (1) EARS provides phrase templates. (2) False — Cohn's user-story structure is also a phrase template, not a form template. (3) Cockburn's use-case structure with predefined fields is a form template. (4) A predefined document structure for a whole specification is a document template. (5) False — it is classified as a form template because it provides predefined fields to fill in; the kind of requirement it specifies (quality vs. functional) does not determine the template category.
questions.reference: EU3.3 — Template-Based Work Products (Phrase, Form, and Document Templates)

questions.prompt: The CityFlex team uses the ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148-style phrase template "`[<Condition>]` `<Subject>` `<Action>` `<Objects>` `[<Restriction>]`." Judge the following statements as true or false.

statements.text: In "When a valid card is sensed, the system shall display the 'Enter your PIN' message on the dialog screen within 200 ms," the bracketed `[<Condition>]` part corresponds to "When a valid card is sensed."
The auxiliary verb "shall" denotes a requirement that is optional and only a suggestion.
"Should" denotes a requirement that is not mandatory but strongly desired.
A sentence using "will," or a present-tense verb without "shall/should/may," is still treated as a binding requirement under this convention.
If a project has not agreed on the meaning of these auxiliary verbs, the syllabus recommends making such definitions explicit as part of the requirements specification.

questions.explanation: (1) Matches the template's condition slot. (2) False — "shall" denotes a mandatory requirement; "may" denotes a suggestion. (3) Correct, as stated in the convention. (4) False — "will" (or a bare present-tense verb) denotes a factual statement, not a requirement. (5) Correct — the syllabus recommends making such verb-meaning definitions explicit in the specification when not already agreed upon.
questions.reference: EU3.3 — Template-Based Work Products (Phrase Templates — ISO 29148)

questions.prompt: According to the syllabus, which of the following is a genuine advantage of representing requirements as models rather than purely in natural language?

options.text: Models eliminate the need for any accompanying natural-language text.
Models can fully express quality requirements and constraints with the same precision as functional requirements.
A model is always self-explanatory, even without a legend, regardless of the notation used.
A restricted modeling syntax reduces possible ambiguities and omissions compared to natural language.
Keeping several models that each focus on a different aspect consistent with each other happens automatically once a modeling tool is used.

questions.explanation: The syllabus states that requirements modeling languages have a restricted syntax, which reduces possible ambiguities and omissions compared with natural language. The other options contradict explicitly stated limitations: models still need accompanying natural-language text, models focus primarily on functional requirements (not quality requirements/constraints), keeping multiple models consistent is described as "challenging" rather than automatic, and non-standard notations require a legend.
questions.reference: EU3.4.1 — The Role of Models in Requirements Engineering

questions.prompt: Which of the following statements about modeling requirements, as described in the syllabus, is **NOT** correct?

options.text: Requirements models and requirements in natural language are frequently combined because not every relevant item of information can be expressed in a model.
Models can be used to validate textually represented requirements with the goal of uncovering omissions, ambiguities, and inconsistencies.
Models reduce the cognitive load of understanding requirements by focusing on a single aspect.
A legend is required when requirements are specified in a non-standard modeling language, explaining the language's syntax and semantics.

Once a complete set of models exists for a system, natural-language requirements become unnecessary, because models can express quality requirements and constraints just as well as functional requirements.

questions.explanation: The syllabus explicitly lists as a limitation that "models focus primarily on functional requirements; most quality requirements and constraints cannot be expressed in models with reasonable effort." Therefore natural language remains necessary even with a complete set of models. Options A, B, C, and D are consistent with the syllabus; E is the incorrect statement.
questions.reference: EU3.4.1 — The Role of Models in Requirements Engineering

questions.prompt: The UrbanWheels car-sharing team is deciding whether to replace its lengthy natural-language requirements document with a set of UML diagrams. Judge the following statements as true or false.

statements.text: A graphic model always makes the requirements easier to validate for every stakeholder, regardless of whether that stakeholder has learned the notation used.
Using several complementary models (e.g., a context model, a class model, and a state model) for UrbanWheels requires extra effort to keep the models consistent with one another.
A UML class diagram for the classes Booking and Vehicle can, by itself, fully and precisely specify the quality requirement "the booking confirmation must be sent within 2 seconds."
Replacing all textual requirements with models removes any further need for natural-language documentation.

questions.explanation: (1) A model only helps a reader who has mastered the modeling language — an unfamiliar notation does not aid understanding. (2) The syllabus names keeping multiple aspect-models consistent as a genuine challenge. (3) Models focus primarily on functional requirements; quality requirements like a response-time constraint are generally not expressible with reasonable effort in a class diagram. (4) The syllabus recommends combining models with natural language, since not everything can be captured in a model's restricted syntax.
questions.reference: EU3.4.1 — The Role of Models in Requirements Engineering

questions.prompt: The UrbanWheels team wants an early, high-level picture that shows the Booking System as a single black box, its boundary, and which external parties — Member, Payment Gateway, Vehicle Telematics Unit, Fleet Operator — exchange which information with it, without detailing any internal functionality yet. Which model type best fits this purpose?

options.text: A context model, e.g. expressed as a context diagram

questions.explanation: Context models specify the structural embedding of a system in its environment and the interaction between the system and the actors in its context, including the interfaces exchanged — exactly the black-box picture UrbanWheels needs at this early stage. Class, state, and activity diagrams, as well as ER diagrams, instead model internal structure, behavior, or flow once the context has already been established.

questions.prompt: Regarding the two common ways to model the UrbanWheels system context — a data-flow-diagram-style context diagram versus a UML use case diagram — name the **two** correct statements.

options.text: The association between an actor and a use case in a UML use case diagram documents the direction of data flow, exactly as a DFD arrow does.
A UML use case diagram cannot depict a system boundary.
There is a single, internationally standardized notation for context diagrams that every RE tool must follow.
A UML use case diagram visualizes the system's functions from the perspective of the actors who interact with it, with a system boundary separating actors from use cases.
Both diagram types are primarily used to describe the state-dependent behavior of individual objects.
A DFD-style context diagram represents the system as a single process (black box) connected to terminators that act as sources and/or sinks of information.

questions.explanation: The syllabus describes DFD context diagrams as representing the system as one process surrounded by terminators (sources/sinks), and UML use case diagrams as showing the system's use cases and actors from a functional perspective, separated by a system boundary. There is no standardized notation for context diagrams (so C is false); a use case association expresses an actor's relationship to a use case, not data-flow direction (so A is false); use case diagrams do show a system boundary (so B is false); and neither diagram type targets state-dependent behavior (so E is false). D and F are correct.

questions.prompt: The UrbanWheels team wants to model which business objects — Member, Vehicle, Booking, Invoice — the system must know about, together with their attributes and relationships (e.g., one Member can place multiple Bookings). Which of the following would be **LEAST** suitable for this modeling purpose?
questions.explanation: Modeling structure and data — the static objects, attributes, and relationships of a domain — is the purpose of UML class diagrams, entity relationship diagrams, and (as a supplementary model type) SysML block definition diagrams. A UML activity diagram instead models the sequence of actions and control flow of a process, which is a function-and-flow concern, not a structure-and-data one.

questions.prompt: The UrbanWheels team needs to specify the sequence of steps — check membership validity, check car availability, confirm the booking, send a confirmation, or follow an alternative flow if no car is available nearby — including which role is responsible for each step. Which model type is best suited for this?
questions.explanation: Activity models specify the sequence of actions required to produce a result from given inputs, including the control flow between actions and who is responsible for each action — precisely what is needed here. UML activity diagrams express activity models. Class, state, context, and ER models instead address structure/data, state/behavior, or system-context concerns.

questions.prompt: The UrbanWheels team wants to specify that a Booking object moves through the stages Requested → Confirmed → Active → Completed, that it can move to Active only after payment succeeds, and that it can be moved to Cancelled from any of the other stages. Which model type is best suited to specify this?
questions.explanation: This describes state-dependent behavior: the states a Booking can take and the events/conditions that trigger transitions between them. State machines model exactly this, and in UML they are expressed as state machine (state) diagrams. A class diagram could list "status" as an attribute but cannot describe the allowed order of transitions; activity and use case diagrams address flow and functional scope, not object life cycles.

questions.prompt: Name the **three** correct pairings below of a modeling perspective with a diagram type the syllabus associates with it.

options.text: State and behavior → UML state machine diagram
Function and flow → UML class diagram
Structure and data → UML activity diagram
Structure and data → UML class diagram
State and behavior → Entity relationship diagram
Function and flow → UML activity diagram

questions.explanation: The syllabus associates structure and data with UML class diagrams (3.4.3), function and flow with UML activity diagrams (3.4.4), and state and behavior with UML state machine diagrams (3.4.5). Options D, E, and F swap the diagram type into the wrong perspective — an activity diagram does not model static structure, a class diagram does not model control flow, and an ER diagram models structure/data, not behavior.

questions.prompt: Which of the following statements about the further (supplementary) model types from the syllabus are true, and which are false?

statements.text: Goal models expressed as AND/OR trees link subgoals to goals, where an OR relationship means that all subgoals must be fulfilled in order to fulfill the goal.
Domain story models use domain-specific symbols to visualize how actors interact with devices and artifacts, helping to understand the application domain.
A UML sequence diagram can only be used to model state and behavior, never function and flow.
SysML block definition diagrams can be adapted to express context models by using stereotyped blocks for the system and its actors.

questions.explanation: (1) An OR relationship means at least one subgoal must be fulfilled; an AND relationship requires all subgoals. (2) This matches the syllabus description of domain story models. (3) The handbook notes a sequence diagram's dynamic aspect "can be function & flow as well as state & behavior," so it serves both purposes. (4) SysML block definition diagrams can be adapted with stereotyped blocks to express context diagrams, as stated in the syllabus.
questions.reference: EU3.4.6 — Further Model Types in Requirements Engineering

questions.prompt: Two UrbanWheels developers use "Member" to mean only a paying subscriber, while a third uses the same word to also include unregistered guest users of the app. This situation primarily illustrates the risk that a glossary is meant to mitigate, namely:

options.text: Lack of conformance to a mandated document template
Lack of necessity of a requirement for the system scope
Lack of traceability between requirements and their origin
Lack of a shared understanding of terminology
Lack of verifiability of a requirement's fulfillment

questions.explanation: The syllabus states that in any RE endeavor involving more than one person there is a risk that people interpret the same term differently; a glossary mitigates exactly this lack of shared understanding of terminology. Traceability, verifiability, conformance, and necessity are unrelated quality criteria that concern requirements or work products, not terminology.

questions.prompt: Name the **three** rules below that the syllabus states for managing the UrbanWheels glossary.

options.text: Make the use of the glossary mandatory.
Only the project manager may ever read the glossary.
Update the glossary only once, at project kickoff.
Allow each sub-team to maintain its own local glossary for flexibility.
Define a person or small group who is responsible for the glossary.

questions.explanation: The syllabus lists managing the glossary centrally, making its use mandatory, and assigning a responsible person or small group as explicit rules. It contradicts B (a single, central glossary is required, not fragmented local ones), D (the glossary must be accessible for everybody involved), and F (the glossary must be maintained over the entire course of system development, not just once).

questions.prompt: At UrbanWheels, the terms "Booking" and "Reservation" are used interchangeably by different teams to refer to exactly the same concept. In glossary terminology, these two terms are:
questions.explanation: Synonyms are different terms denoting the same thing, which should be marked as such in the glossary; this matches "Booking" and "Reservation" referring to the same concept. Homonyms are the opposite case — one term used for different things — and abbreviations/acronyms are shortened forms of a term, not a pair of interchangeable terms.

questions.prompt: Before any detailed requirements exist, UrbanWheels management wants a short, conceptual description of the future car-sharing app's key characteristics and the value it will create for its users, in order to pitch the idea to investors. Which document type best fits this need?
questions.explanation: A vision document is a conceptual description of a future system's key characteristics and the value it creates for its users — exactly what is needed for an early investor pitch, before detailed requirements exist. A system requirements specification and user requirements specification presuppose detailed, elicited requirements, a business requirements specification focuses on organizational goals rather than the system's characteristics, and a sprint backlog is an agile work-item list, not a conceptual pitch document.
questions.reference: EU3.6 — Requirements Documents and Documentation Structures

questions.prompt: The UrbanWheels product owner wants to show exactly which prioritized work items the team commits to build during the next two-week iteration only. Which of the following would be **LEAST** appropriate for this specific purpose?
questions.explanation: A sprint backlog is precisely defined as a selected subset of a product backlog with work items to be realized in the next iteration, making it the natural fit; a story map or the full product backlog could still plausibly support that view. A classic, heavyweight system requirements specification is not designed to express an iteration-scoped commitment and is the least appropriate choice here.
questions.reference: EU3.6 — Requirements Documents and Documentation Structures

questions.prompt: Judge the following statements about choosing a documentation structure for UrbanWheels as true or false.

statements.text: The choice of documentation structure may legitimately depend on a contractual clause that prescribes a specific document template.
Once a documentation structure has been used successfully in one project, the syllabus recommends always reusing it unchanged in every future project, regardless of context.
The size of the requirements document is one of the factors that influences how much internal structure the document needs.
The chosen software development process (e.g., agile versus plan-driven) has no bearing on which documentation structure is appropriate.

questions.explanation: (1) The contract is explicitly named as a factor, since a customer may prescribe a given structure. (2) Documents or structures "should not be reused from previous projects without reflection." (3) Document size is explicitly listed as a factor — larger documents need more structure. (4) The chosen development process is explicitly listed as a factor influencing the documentation structure.
questions.reference: EU3.6 — Requirements Documents and Documentation Structures

questions.prompt: An UrbanWheels UX designer sketches rough screens on paper, with boxes labeled "map," "car list," and "confirm button," to discuss layout ideas with stakeholders in a workshop, deliberately keeping the sketch unpolished and quick to redraw. This is best classified as:
questions.explanation: Wireframes are low-fidelity prototypes built with simple materials or sketching tools, built quickly, modified easily, and deliberately not polished — serving to discuss and validate UI concepts. A mock-up uses real screens and click flows, a native prototype implements real functionality, and an evolutionary prototype is a pilot system that forms the core of the final product, none of which matches a quick paper sketch.

questions.prompt: Which **two** of the following statements about exploratory prototypes, as described in the syllabus, are correct?

options.text: They are used to create shared understanding, clarify requirements, or validate requirements at different levels of fidelity.
Only high-fidelity prototypes count as exploratory prototypes; wireframes and mock-ups belong to a separate category.
They always require a working backend integration to be useful.
They always implement the full functionality of the final system.
They are pilot systems that incrementally evolve into the final system.

questions.explanation: The syllabus describes exploratory prototypes as used to create shared understanding, clarify, or validate requirements at different levels of fidelity, and as discarded after use. Statements D describes evolutionary prototypes instead; B, E, and F misdescribe exploratory prototypes, which range from low- to high-fidelity (wireframes, mock-ups, and native prototypes are all exploratory prototype types) and do not require full functionality or a working backend.

questions.prompt: Which of the following statements about native prototypes is **INCORRECT**?

options.text: They are primarily used for low-cost, quick-and-dirty discussion of UI layout ideas before any real design has been considered.
They are high-fidelity prototypes that implement critical parts of the system.
They let stakeholders assess whether the prototyped part of the system will work and behave as expected.
They can be used to explore and decide between different requirements variants for some aspect of the system.

questions.explanation: Describing low-cost, quick-and-dirty UI layout discussion is a description of wireframes, not native prototypes. Native prototypes are high-fidelity, implement critical parts of the system to assess real behavior, and can also be used to explore design/requirements variants — all of which are correctly stated in A, B, and D.

questions.prompt: Judge the following statements about UrbanWheels prototyping activities as true or false.

statements.text: A wireframe of the UrbanWheels booking screen is typically built quickly and deliberately does not resemble a polished final product.
A mock-up of the car-unlock flow provides real, working backend functionality that actually unlocks a car.
An evolutionary prototype forms a pilot system that is incrementally extended into the final UrbanWheels app, an approach frequently used in agile development.
Prototyping is essentially cost-free, so a Requirements Engineer never needs to weigh its cost against the value gained.

questions.explanation: (1) Matches the definition of a wireframe exactly. (2) Mock-ups use real screens and click flows but without real functionality — unlocking a real car would require a native prototype. (3) Matches the definition of an evolutionary prototype, which agile development frequently employs. (4) The syllabus explicitly notes a trade-off between the cost of building/using a prototype and the value gained.

questions.prompt: A reviewer finds the following requirement in the UrbanWheels system requirements specification: "The app shall unlock the reserved car in a user-friendly way." Which quality criterion for single requirements is most clearly violated?
questions.explanation: "User-friendly" has no shared, agreed-upon meaning — different readers will interpret it differently, which is exactly what the Unambiguous criterion (a true shared understanding of the requirement) addresses. One could also argue it is hard to verify, but the root cause is the vague, ambiguous qualifier, not a dispute over scope (Necessary), truthfulness to stakeholder needs (Adequate), or missing self-contained information (Complete).
questions.reference: EU3.8 — Quality Criteria for Work Products and Requirements

questions.prompt: The UrbanWheels system requirements specification contains the requirement: "The system shall process the request as described in the workshop notes from March 3rd." The referenced workshop notes were never attached to the specification and are unavailable to most readers of the document. Name the **two** quality criteria for single requirements that are most clearly violated.
questions.explanation: The requirement is not self-contained, since it depends on external information (the workshop notes) that is missing from the document — a violation of Complete. Because most readers cannot access that referenced material, the target audience cannot fully comprehend the requirement either — a violation of Understandable. It is not primarily about truthfulness to stakeholder needs (Adequate), scope (Necessary), ambiguity of wording (Unambiguous), or checkability (Verifiable).
questions.reference: EU3.8 — Quality Criteria for Work Products and Requirements

questions.prompt: Stakeholders never requested it, and it does not contribute to any stated UrbanWheels business goal, yet a developer adds the requirement: "The app shall display a rotating banner of car manufacturer logos on the home screen." Which quality criterion for single requirements is violated?
questions.explanation: Necessary means the requirement is part of the relevant system scope and contributes to at least one stakeholder goal or need; a requirement nobody asked for and that serves no goal fails this criterion. The requirement may be stated clearly and even be truthfully describable (so Unambiguous and Adequate are not the issue here), and verifiability is not the problem — whether or not the banner exists can be checked easily.
questions.reference: EU3.8 — Quality Criteria for Work Products and Requirements

questions.prompt: Name the **three** quality criteria below that the syllabus defines for RE work products covering multiple requirements, as opposed to criteria for single requirements.
questions.explanation: Consistent, Non-redundant, and Traceable (together with Complete, Modifiable, and Conformant) are the quality criteria the syllabus specifies for work products covering more than one requirement. Adequate, Unambiguous, and Verifiable instead belong to the set of quality criteria for single requirements.
questions.reference: EU3.8 — Quality Criteria for Work Products and Requirements

questions.prompt: For each statement about a documented UrbanWheels requirement or work product, judge whether the identified quality-criterion violation is correctly diagnosed (True) or incorrectly diagnosed (False).

statements.text: Two UrbanWheels requirements documents state different cancellation-fee amounts for the same scenario; this is correctly diagnosed as a violation of Consistency.

A damage-reporting rule is documented twice — once in the vision document, once in the system requirements specification — using different wording; this is correctly diagnosed as a violation of Verifiability.
A requirement for "fast car unlocking" cannot be checked against any measurable threshold; this is correctly diagnosed as a violation of Verifiability.
The UrbanWheels requirements document does not follow the company-mandated document template structure; this is correctly diagnosed as a violation of Conformance.
A requirement is written using technical jargon unfamiliar to the business stakeholders who must approve it; this is correctly diagnosed as a violation of Traceability.

questions.explanation: (1) Contradicting statements across documents is exactly what Consistent addresses. (2) Documenting the same rule twice is a Non-redundant violation, not a Verifiability one. (3) "Fast" with no measurable threshold cannot be indisputably checked, which is a Verifiable violation. (4) Failing to follow a mandatory template structure is exactly what Conformant addresses. (5) Jargon unfamiliar to the approving audience is an Understandable violation, not a Traceable one.
questions.reference: EU3.8 — Quality Criteria for Work Products and Requirements

questions.prompt: The UrbanWheels requirements are organized as one large, unstructured document. Every small change to the cancellation policy requires re-reading and manually adjusting dozens of unrelated sections, which is slow and error-prone. Which quality criterion for work products is placed most at risk by this documentation style?
questions.explanation: Modifiable means the work product is set up so that it can be modified without degrading its quality; a poorly structured document that forces scattered, error-prone manual edits for a single change clearly fails this criterion. The scenario does not describe duplicate statements of the same requirement (Non-redundant), broken links to origins/implementations (Traceable), or a mismatch with a mandated format (Conformant).
questions.reference: EU3.8 — Quality Criteria for Work Products and Requirements

questions.prompt: Six months after release, nobody at UrbanWheels can say which stakeholder originally requested the "loyalty discount" feature, nor is there any test case that could confirm whether the implemented system actually fulfills it. Name the **two** quality criteria that are most clearly violated here.
questions.explanation: The inability to trace the requirement back to the stakeholder who requested it is a violation of Traceable (traceability to origins). The absence of any test case that could indisputably confirm fulfillment is a violation of Verifiable. The scenario says nothing about whether the requirement's intent is true to stakeholder needs (Adequate), in scope (Necessary), ambiguous (Unambiguous), contradicted elsewhere (Consistent), or hard to edit (Modifiable).
questions.reference: EU3.8 — Quality Criteria for Work Products and Requirements

questions.prompt: Judge the following statements about applying quality criteria in modern, value-oriented Requirements Engineering as true or false.

statements.text: According to the syllabus, all quality criteria must always be fully satisfied for every requirement, regardless of the value that requirement creates.

Adequacy and understandability are considered the most important quality criteria for single requirements, because without them a requirement is useless or even harmful, regardless of whether all other criteria are met.
Verifiability becomes particularly important when the implemented system must undergo a formal acceptance procedure.
The higher the value a requirement creates, the less important it becomes to satisfy its quality criteria.

questions.explanation: (1) In a value-oriented approach, the degree of fulfillment of a quality criterion should correspond to the value created by the requirement — requirements do not have to adhere to all criteria completely. (2) The syllabus names adequacy and understandability as the most important criteria for exactly this reason. (3) Verifiability is explicitly called out as important for formal acceptance procedures. (4) The relationship is the opposite: the higher the value, the more relevant the quality criteria become, to reduce the risk of failure.
questions.reference: EU3.8 — Quality Criteria for Work Products and Requirements

chapters.title: Sources for Requirements & Elicitation of Requirements / Resolving Conflicts regarding Requirements & Validation of Requirements

questions.prompt:
While scoping CarShare24, UrbanWheels's requirements engineer is deciding which of four candidate entities should actually be investigated as a requirements source, based on whether they lie in the system's context (interact with, interface to, or influence the system while remaining otherwise unchanged by the project).

Which of the following should be treated as a genuine requirements source?

options.text: The number of parking spaces in a shopping-mall garage that no CarShare24 vehicle ever uses
The internal database table the development team itself designs to store a vehicle's mileage
