Statements A, C, and D correctly state the definitions of functional requirement, constraint, and quality requirement.

questions.prompt: Per the syllabus (EU 4.1), which THREE of the following are listed as typical stakeholder roles for a system such as ParcelPath?

options.text: Anonymous online reviewers of unrelated products

questions.explanation: The syllabus lists Users, Sponsors, Managers, Developers, Authorities, and Customers as typical stakeholder roles (EU 4.1). Competitors' marketing departments, anonymous reviewers of unrelated products, and a database schema are not stakeholders of the system at all.

questions.prompt: A ParcelPath business analyst writes four statements. For each, decide whether it is TRUE or FALSE that the given sentence illustrates the named requirements aspect (EU 3.1.4).

statements.text: "A Shipment consists of one or more Parcels, and each Parcel belongs to exactly one Shipment." illustrates the structure and data aspect.
"After the warehouse picker confirms the pick list, the system generates a packing slip and then notifies the carrier dispatch queue." illustrates the function and flow aspect.
"While a parcel is in the state Out-for-Delivery, the courier app shall disable the 'cancel order' button." illustrates the context aspect.

"The ParcelPath system shall exchange a tracking-number confirmation message with the SwiftVan Logistics carrier system when a parcel is handed off." illustrates the context aspect (system boundary and external interfaces).

questions.explanation: (1) Object relationships/cardinalities are structure and data. (2) A sequence of actions and control flow between them is function and flow. (3) A state-dependent reaction ("while in state X, disable Y") is the state and behavior aspect, not context — so statement 3 is false. (4) An exchange with an external actor across the system boundary is the context aspect.
questions.reference: EU3.1.4 — Aspects to be Considered in Work Products

questions.prompt:
The ParcelPath team debates whether to add a "predicted delivery window" feature with sub-minute precision tracking. Building and validating this precision would cost far more effort than the extra benefit it brings to shoppers, who are satisfied with a 30-minute window.

Which RE principle (EU 2.2) most directly applies to this debate?
questions.explanation: Value-orientation defines a requirement's value as its benefit minus the cost of eliciting, documenting, validating, and managing it; here the cost of the extra precision clearly outweighs the marginal benefit to shoppers. Innovation (C) concerns exceeding expectations, not cost/benefit trade-offs, and is the weaker fit here.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is NOT part of the information that should be documented for each stakeholder in a stakeholder list, according to the syllabus (EU 4.1)?

options.text: Temporal and spatial availability during the project
Goals and interests in terms of the project
The stakeholder's personal salary and performance review history

questions.explanation: The syllabus's recommended stakeholder-list fields are name, function/role, contact data, temporal/spatial availability, relevance, expertise, and goals/interests — personal salary or performance history is not among them and is irrelevant to RE.

questions.prompt: A ParcelPath Requirements Engineer is deciding how much detail to specify for a new "delivery exception handling" feature. According to the syllabus (EU 3.1.3), which THREE factors should influence the chosen level of detail?

options.text: The degree of freedom to be left to the designers and programmers
The number of competing e-commerce platforms in the market
The personal preference of the Requirements Engineer for long documents
The degree of shared understanding already achieved about the problem among the team
Availability of rapid stakeholder feedback during design and implementation
The size of the Requirements Engineering team

questions.explanation: The syllabus names the problem/development context, degree of shared understanding, degree of freedom left to designers/programmers, availability of rapid stakeholder feedback, cost vs. value, and imposed standards/regulations as factors influencing level of detail. Market competition, personal preference, and team size are not listed factors.

questions.prompt:
ParcelPath's delivery-tracking backlog changes weekly based on live carrier feedback and shopper usage data. Stakeholders (product owner, carriers, support leads) are available continuously, and the team runs two-week sprints indefinitely, adding and revising requirements each iteration.

Which RE process time facet (EU 5.2) best fits this setting?
questions.explanation: Requirements emerging and evolving incrementally, continuously available stakeholders enabling short feedback loops, and a development spanning many iterations are exactly the criteria the syllabus gives for choosing an iterative RE process, as opposed to a linear one specified up front.

questions.prompt: A ParcelPath business analyst drafts the requirement: "The relevant people shall be notified faster when a parcel is delayed." Which TWO natural-language pitfalls (EU 3.2) are present in this requirement?

options.text: Incomplete comparison ("faster" without stating a baseline to compare against)
Incomplete description (an entire necessary clause is missing)
Nominalization turning a verb into an ambiguous noun
Unspecific noun ("the relevant people" without naming the stakeholder role)
Universal quantifier overgeneralizing across all cases

questions.explanation: "The relevant people" is an unspecific noun that fails to name a concrete stakeholder role, and "faster" is an incomplete comparison with no stated baseline. There is no missing conditional clause (C), no universal quantifier like "all"/"never" (D), no nominalization (E), and no entirely missing clause (F).

questions.prompt:
ParcelPath integrates with SwiftVan Logistics' public tracking API to receive scan events after a parcel is handed off. ParcelPath has no control over SwiftVan's internal warehouse software but must understand its behavior to interpret the scan events correctly.

From ParcelPath's RE perspective (EU 2.2, Principle 4 — Context), where does SwiftVan's internal warehouse software belong?

options.text: Inside the system boundary of the ParcelPath platform
Inside the system context, but outside the system boundary, because the scan events it generates are relevant to understanding ParcelPath's requirements
It constitutes a constraint rather than a context element
Outside the context boundary entirely, and therefore irrelevant to ParcelPath's RE

questions.explanation: SwiftVan's internal warehouse software is not part of the ParcelPath system (outside the system boundary) but is part of the relevant environment needed to understand ParcelPath's requirements (inside the system context), since the scan events it produces matter to ParcelPath's behavior. Determining what lies inside vs. outside the system boundary, using the context, is a core elicitation-preparation task (EO 4.1.1).

questions.prompt: Ahead of the Q3 release, ParcelPath freezes a specific, consistent set of versions of its requirements work products (exactly one version per work product) as the stable basis for release planning; no further changes are allowed without formal change control. Judge each statement (EU 6.3, 6.4) as TRUE or FALSE.

statements.text: This frozen set is an example of a baseline, since a baseline is a stable, change-controlled configuration used for release planning.
Every requirements configuration is automatically a baseline, whether or not it has been stabilized or change-controlled.
A configuration may contain more than one version of the same work product at the same time.
Version control requires, among other things, a version number and a documented history of what was changed.

questions.explanation: (1) This is exactly the definition of a baseline. (2) Not every configuration is stabilized/change-controlled, so not every configuration is a baseline. (3) A configuration contains at most one version of each work product, so statement 3 is false. (4) Version control indeed requires a version number and a history of changes (plus a storage concept).

questions.prompt: Judge each statement about writing natural-language requirements (EU 3.2) as TRUE or FALSE.

statements.text: Passive voice should always be avoided entirely in natural-language requirements, per the syllabus.
Universal quantifiers such as "all" or "never" are listed among items to be used with care, not among items to strictly avoid.
Incomplete conditions (e.g., omitting the "only if" clause) are listed among the things to avoid, not the things to use with care.
Nominalizations, i.e., nouns derived from a verb such as "authentication," are listed among the things to avoid entirely.

questions.explanation: Passive voice, universal quantifiers, and nominalizations are listed as things to be "used with care," not strictly avoided — so statement 1 is false and statement 2 is true. Incomplete conditions are listed among the things to avoid outright, making statement 3 true. Nominalizations are not in the "avoid" list, so statement 4 is false.

questions.prompt:
ParcelPath's RE team needs to decide, when integrating a third-party carrier API, where to draw the line between what is relevant environment for understanding ParcelPath's requirements and what is simply "the rest of the world" that need not be analyzed at all.

Which of the following statements about Principle 4 (Context, EU 2.2) and related terms is **NOT** correct?

options.text: The context boundary and the system boundary are two names for exactly the same concept and can be used interchangeably
The context boundary separates the RE-relevant part of a system's environment from the rest of the world that need not be analyzed — precisely the line ParcelPath's team is drawing here
The system boundary separates the system itself from its surrounding context
A context model is a type of model used to document a system's environment and its interfaces to that environment

questions.explanation: The context boundary and system boundary are distinct concepts: the context boundary marks the edge of the RE-relevant environment versus "the rest of the world," while the system boundary marks the edge of the system itself versus its context — they are not interchangeable. Statements B, C, and D are all accurate.

questions.prompt:
During a design-thinking workshop, ParcelPath discovers that shoppers who experience a feature letting them redirect an in-transit parcel to a nearby pickup locker (a feature they never explicitly asked for) become noticeably more loyal, while shoppers who don't get it do not complain about its absence at all.

Per the Kano model (EU 4.2), this feature is best classified as a:
questions.explanation: A delighter (excitement factor, unconscious requirement) is a feature customers did not ask for but which attracts and delights them when present, while its absence causes no complaints — exactly as described. A dissatisfier behaves the opposite way (its absence causes outrage), and a satisfier is explicitly requested by customers.

questions.prompt:
ParcelPath wants to specify: "When the courier's handheld scanner detects a valid parcel barcode at hand-off, the carrier-integration module shall update the shipment status to 'In Transit.'"

Which EARS phrase template type (EU 3.3.1) does this requirement follow?
questions.explanation: The phrase follows "WHEN <trigger> the <system> shall <response>," the EARS template for requirements triggered by an external event (the barcode scan). It is not a ubiquitous requirement (no trigger needed), not an IF...THEN unwanted-behavior requirement, and not a WHILE/WHERE template.

questions.prompt: According to the syllabus (EU 1.2), which THREE of the following are typical causes of inadequate Requirements Engineering?

options.text: The assumption that requirements are self-evident
Rushing straight into building the system without proper RE
Using a glossary to align terminology across teams
Hiring experienced Requirements Engineers for the project
Spending too much time on stakeholder workshops early in the project

questions.explanation: The syllabus names rushing straight into building, communication problems, and the assumption that requirements are self-evident (alongside inadequate RE education, not offered here) as typical causes of inadequate RE. More stakeholder workshops, experienced engineers, and glossary use are good practices, not causes of inadequate RE.

questions.prompt:
ParcelPath shoppers never explicitly ask for order-confirmation emails; however, if these emails were missing, shoppers would be upset and would consider the platform broken.

Per the Kano model (EU 4.2), order-confirmation emails are a:
questions.explanation: A dissatisfier (basic factor, subconscious requirement) is so obvious that customers do not ask for it, but its absence causes strong dissatisfaction — matching confirmation emails exactly. A delighter's absence would not be noticed; a satisfier is explicitly requested.

questions.prompt:
ParcelPath specifies: "IF the carrier-integration module receives a shipment-status update for a tracking number that does not exist in ParcelPath's order database, THEN the module shall reject the update and log an error."

Which EARS requirement type (EU 3.3.1) is this?
questions.explanation: The "IF <precondition> <trigger>, THEN the <system> shall <response>" structure is the EARS template specifically for unwanted behavior — situations to be avoided, such as invalid input. It differs from the event-driven "WHEN" template, which is used for expected/desired triggers rather than unwanted ones.

questions.prompt:
ParcelPath's RE lead is evaluating whether to introduce a dedicated requirements-management tool to replace spreadsheets for tracking the delivery-tracking backlog.

Per the syllabus (EU 7.2), which of the following is **NOT** a pitfall to avoid when selecting and introducing such a tool?

options.text: Selecting the tool that the most competitors use, rather than one that fits ParcelPath's own RE process
Choosing a tool based primarily on its license cost rather than its fit for purpose
Ensuring that proper RE procedures, techniques, and responsibilities are already established before searching for an appropriate tool
Rolling the tool out to the entire organization immediately, without first establishing proper RE procedures, techniques, and responsibilities

questions.explanation: The syllabus states that an appropriate tool can only be sought once proper RE procedures, techniques, and responsibilities are already established — so doing this first is the recommended practice, not a pitfall. Selecting by popularity (A), by cost alone (B), and rolling out broadly without first establishing RE procedures (D) are the genuine pitfalls to avoid.

questions.prompt:
A ParcelPath user story reads: "As a shopper, I want to see a live map of my courier's location." It has no stated benefit and no acceptance criteria attached.

Per the syllabus (EU 3.3.1), what is the most important consequence of omitting acceptance criteria for this user story?

options.text: The implementation is more likely to be accepted inconsistently, because the concrete, testable criteria for "done" are missing, increasing the risk of misunderstanding
The user story automatically becomes a durable work product
The user story no longer follows Cohn's phrase template at all
The user story becomes more concrete and easier to estimate

questions.explanation: Acceptance criteria make a user story more concrete and testable; without them, there is no agreed definition of "done," increasing the risk that implementation will not match stakeholder expectations. The story still follows Cohn's phrase structure (so C is not the consequence), while B and D do not describe the risk of omitting acceptance criteria.

questions.prompt: For each technique below, decide whether the statement is TRUE or FALSE, where TRUE means "classified by the syllabus (EU 4.2) as a gathering technique" and FALSE means "classified as a design-and-idea-generating technique."

statements.text: Conducting structured interviews with warehouse pickers about their current workflow is a gathering technique.
Running a brainstorming session to invent new delivery-exception features is a gathering technique.
Building a storyboard that depicts a shopper's exception-handling journey when a delivery fails is a gathering technique.
Observing warehouse pickers at work without interfering, to learn their undocumented tacit routines, is a gathering technique.

questions.explanation: Interviews (questioning) and observation are gathering-technique categories (statements 1 and 4 are true). Brainstorming and storyboards are design-and-idea-generating techniques intended to stimulate creativity, not gathering techniques (statements 2 and 3 are false).

questions.prompt:
A customer-support agent at ParcelPath wants to find out which original stakeholder request led to the "redirect to pickup locker" requirement, while a tester wants to find which test cases verify that same requirement.

These two needs correspond respectively to (EU 6.6):
questions.explanation: Tracing a requirement back to its origin is backward traceability; tracing it forward to subsequent work products such as test cases is forward traceability — matching the support agent's and tester's needs respectively.

questions.prompt: Which THREE of the following are genuine fields of Cockburn's form template for use cases, as presented in the syllabus (EU 3.3.2)?
questions.explanation: Cockburn's use case form template includes fields such as Name, Precondition, Success/Failed end condition, Primary actor, Other actors, Trigger, Normal flow, Alternate flows, Extensions, and Related information — Trigger, Primary actor, and Precondition are genuine fields. "Database index," "Marketing persona," and "ROI estimate" are not part of the template.

questions.prompt:
ParcelPath cannot interview every individual shopper, so the RE team defines a fictional archetypical description, "Busy Parent Priya," to represent a group of shoppers with similar needs.

What is this technique called (EU 2.2, Principle 2 — Stakeholders)?
questions.explanation: A persona is a fictional, archetypical description used as a substitute when a stakeholder role has too many individuals or when individuals are unknown — exactly the case described for "Busy Parent Priya."

questions.prompt:
A ParcelPath Requirements Engineer spends two days physically working alongside a warehouse picker, performing the picking tasks under supervision to learn the job from the inside, rather than just watching.

This is an example of which gathering technique (EU 4.2)?
questions.explanation: Apprenticing is participatory — the Requirements Engineer performs the job themselves under supervision — which distinguishes it from field observation, where the engineer watches without interfering.

questions.prompt:
In the early phase of specifying the planned "Delivery Tracking Service," before any concrete use cases are written, ParcelPath's RE team wants to (a) sketch which external actors and systems the new service will exchange information with, and (b) capture the business goals the new service should help achieve and how those goals relate to each other.

Which TWO model types (EU 3.4) are best suited for these two early-phase needs respectively?
questions.explanation: Context models specify a system's actors and interfaces with its environment, fitting the first need; goal models represent goals, sub-goals, and their relationships, fitting the second need. Class, activity, and statechart models address structure/data, function/flow, and state/behavior respectively — not these two early-phase concerns.
questions.reference: EU3.4.6 — Further Model Types in Requirements Engineering

questions.prompt: Judge each statement about configuring an RE process (EU 5.2) as TRUE or FALSE.

statements.text: A market-oriented RE process combines well with a linear and prescriptive configuration.
Explorative RE processes are typically also iterative processes, and vice versa.
Linear RE processes work only if a sophisticated process for changing requirements is in place.
When outsourcing system development, a prescriptive RE process is always strictly required, and an explorative process can never be used for an outsourcing contract.

questions.explanation: The syllabus explicitly states the market-oriented facet does not combine well with linear/prescriptive facets (statement 1 false). Explorative processes are typically also iterative, and vice versa (statement 2 true). Linear processes require a sophisticated change process (statement 3 true). The syllabus explicitly notes that outsourcing contracts can also be negotiated based on an explorative process, so prescriptive is not "always strictly required" (statement 4 false).

questions.prompt: In a UML class diagram for ParcelPath, the class Shipment is associated with Parcel with a multiplicity of 1 on the Shipment side and 1..* on the Parcel side; Shipment is also associated with Courier with a multiplicity of 0..1 on the Courier side. Judge each statement about this model (EU 3.4.3) as TRUE or FALSE.

statements.text: Each Parcel is associated with exactly one Shipment.
Each Shipment must contain at least one Parcel.
A Shipment may exist without any Courier currently assigned to it.
A single Courier may be assigned to at most one Shipment at any given time, according to this model.

questions.explanation: Multiplicity 1 at the Shipment end means each Parcel links to exactly one Shipment (true); 1..* at the Parcel end means each Shipment has at least one Parcel (true); 0..1 at the Courier end means a Shipment may have zero or one Courier (true). The model says nothing about how many Shipments a single Courier may be linked to at once, since that constraint would be expressed by the multiplicity on the Shipment end of the Courier association, which was not given — so statement 4 cannot be concluded and is false.

questions.prompt:
ParcelPath's warehouse-ops manager insists that same-day pickup confirmations are "obviously" sent via SMS, while the customer-support lead insists they are "obviously" sent via the in-app inbox. Each assumed their own channel was already agreed, and both cite the same never-written-down sprint-planning conversation as their source.

What type of requirements conflict is this (EU 4.3.2)?
questions.explanation: Both parties refer to the same underlying (unwritten) source but interpret it inconsistently — the defining feature of a data conflict. It is not a subject matter conflict (no genuinely different factual needs across contexts) nor a value or structural conflict.

questions.prompt: Per the syllabus's description of the major tasks of RE (EU 1.4), which TWO of the following activities are considered to be part of requirements elicitation rather than separate RE tasks?
questions.explanation: The syllabus states that requirements analysis and requirements conflict resolution are considered to be part of elicitation, distinct from the separate major tasks of documentation, validation, and management.

questions.prompt:
ParcelPath wants to model the warehouse picking process: a picker receives a pick list and walks the aisles to collect items, while in parallel a second picker independently retrieves items from cold storage; both must finish before packing starts.

Which UML activity diagram element (EU 3.4.4) is essential to correctly express this requirement?

options.text: A guard condition on a single transition

questions.explanation: Two independent activities that both must complete before a subsequent activity (packing) begins is modeled with a fork (splitting into parallel flows) and a join (synchronizing them) in a UML activity diagram. A decision node models alternative (not parallel) paths, and a guard condition alone cannot express true concurrency.

questions.prompt:
The ParcelPath product owner wants a report that shows, for every currently open requirement in the backlog, only the requirement ID, priority, and status columns (omitting all other attributes), sorted by priority.

Which TWO view types (EU 6.5) are combined to produce this report?
questions.explanation: Filtering to only open requirements is a selective view; showing only the ID/priority/status columns is a projective view. There is no summarizing or totaling involved, so it is not an aggregating view, and "exploratory" and "native" are not defined view types.

questions.prompt:
The product owner wants to prioritize a flashy "gamified delivery tracker" feature to maximize short-term engagement metrics, while a senior Requirements Engineer insists ParcelPath should prioritize accessibility improvements because every customer deserves equal access regardless of metrics. Both parties are adamant and unwilling to compromise, citing deeply held convictions rather than project facts.

What type of conflict is this (EU 4.3.2)?
questions.explanation: The dispute is rooted in stable, deeply held principles ("every customer deserves equal access") rather than short-term positions or facts, and both sides are unwilling to give up their stance — the hallmark of a value conflict, which the syllabus notes is notoriously difficult to resolve. An interest conflict would instead be driven by more negotiable personal, group, or role-based goals.

questions.prompt:
ParcelPath models a Parcel's lifecycle with states Placed, Picked, Packed, HandedToCarrier, InTransit, OutForDelivery, Delivered, DeliveryFailed, and Returned. The business rule is that the courier app shall only enable the "mark delivered" action while the parcel is in state OutForDelivery.

Which modeling concept (EU 3.4.5) captures this rule?

options.text: A state-driven reaction expressed via a state machine

questions.explanation: A rule that restricts an action to only being available while the system/component is in a specific state is a state-dependent reaction, modeled with a state machine (state and behavior aspect). It is not a class relationship, activity fork, or context interface.

questions.prompt: Judge each statement about the nine RE principles (EU 2.2) as TRUE or FALSE.

statements.text: According to the Evolution principle, Requirements Engineers should aim to keep requirements completely frozen once agreed, since change indicates poor initial elicitation.
The Validation principle states that non-validated requirements are useless, and validation must begin only after the system has been deployed.
The Innovation principle suggests that merely satisfying stakeholders' stated requirements is not enough; good RE strives to make stakeholders happy, excited, or feel safe.
The Systematic and Disciplined Work principle implies that a Requirements Engineer should reuse the exact same RE process from a previous successful project without reflection, to save time.

The Shared Understanding principle distinguishes explicit shared understanding, achieved through documented and agreed requirements, from implicit shared understanding based on shared knowledge, culture, and context.

questions.explanation: Evolution treats change as normal and requires balancing permitting change with keeping requirements stable, not freezing them (1 false). Validation must start already during RE, not only after deployment (2 false). Innovation is correctly described as striving to make stakeholders happy, excited, or feel safe, beyond mere satisfaction (3 true). Systematic and disciplined work explicitly warns against reusing past processes without reflection (4 false). Shared understanding is correctly split into explicit and implicit forms as described (5 true).

questions.prompt:
The ParcelPath RE team wants to (1) visually capture how a frustrated shopper interacts with the "report missing parcel" customer-support desk using domain-specific pictograms, for better domain understanding, and (2) show the precise time-ordered sequence of messages exchanged between the Courier App, the Carrier API, and the Order Service during a hand-off.

Which TWO model types (EU 3.4.6) are best suited for these two needs respectively?
questions.explanation: Domain story models use domain-specific symbols to depict how actors interact with artifacts in a domain, fitting the support-desk story; interaction models (UML sequence diagrams) show the precise time-ordered sequence of messages between objects/actors, fitting the hand-off message exchange. Goal, class, and context models do not address either of these two specific needs.
questions.reference: EU3.4.6 — Further Model Types in Requirements Engineering

questions.prompt:
Two ParcelPath stakeholders disagree over which carrier-integration vendor should supply real-time GPS pings; both options are technically acceptable, but the team cannot reach consensus through discussion. The RE lead lets the whole steering group cast ballots and proceeds with the majority choice.

Which conflict resolution technique (EU 4.3.3) was applied?
questions.explanation: Letting the group cast ballots and following the majority outcome is the defining feature of the voting conflict-resolution technique, distinct from compromise (mutual concession), overruling (one party simply decides), or defining separate variants.

questions.prompt:
ParcelPath's supplier and in-house product team collaborate closely; stakeholders (warehouse ops, support leads) are strongly involved in both the RE and development process, the backlog consists of user stories and prototypes, and information flows continuously between the product owner, Requirements Engineers, and developers.

Which typical RE process configuration (EU 5.3) is this?

options.text: A combination that has no named configuration in the syllabus

questions.explanation: Close supplier–customer collaboration, strong and continuous stakeholder involvement, a backlog of user stories/prototypes, and continuous information flow among product owner, engineers, and developers are exactly the hallmarks the syllabus gives for the Participatory RE Process (iterative, explorative, customer-specific).
questions.reference: EU5.3 — Configuring a Requirements Engineering Process

questions.prompt:
Two ParcelPath teams use the term "Shipment" differently: the warehouse team means "everything picked for one carrier pickup run," while customer support means "a single customer's order, however it is split across parcels."

Which of the following statements about this situation and related terminology (EU 3.5) is **NOT** correct?

options.text: This is an example of a homonym — the same term used to mean two different things
A synonym, by contrast, is when two different terms are used to refer to the same thing
The syllabus recommends that homonyms be avoided, or at least explicitly flagged, in a project glossary
The syllabus does not discuss nominalization (turning a verb into a noun, e.g. "authentication") anywhere, since it is unrelated to writing clear natural-language requirements

questions.explanation: Nominalization (turning a verb into a noun, e.g. "authentication") is explicitly listed in the syllabus as a natural-language writing pitfall to be used with care, since it can obscure who performs an action — it is not absent from the syllabus or irrelevant to requirements clarity. Statements A, B, and C correctly describe homonyms, synonyms, and the glossary guidance to flag or avoid homonyms.
questions.reference: EU3.5 — Glossaries (cross-referencing EU3.2 — Natural-Language-Based Work Products)

questions.prompt:
A ParcelPath warehouse-ops stakeholder requests a late change to how partial-shipment splitting works, two days before the current sprint ends. ParcelPath uses Scrum with a continuously groomed product backlog and no formal Change Control Board.

Per the syllabus (EU 6.7), how should this change most appropriately be handled?

options.text: The product owner adds the change as a new backlog item and prioritizes it for a future sprint
The change can only be implemented if a formally released baseline is first created
The change request must wait for the next linear requirements phase
The change must be submitted to a Change Advisory Board for approval before any backlog update

questions.explanation: In an iterative approach without a Change Control/Advisory Board, the syllabus states the product owner includes the change as a new product backlog item and prioritizes it accordingly, rather than routing it through a formal board or waiting for a linear phase that does not exist in this context.

questions.prompt: Which TWO of the following are exploratory validation techniques rather than review techniques, per the syllabus (EU 4.4)?
questions.explanation: Alpha testing and building an MVP are exploratory techniques, giving stakeholders hands-on experience with a working version of the system. Walkthroughs, inspections, and formal moderated checklist reviews are review techniques, not exploratory ones.

questions.prompt:
ParcelPath runs a fast-moving agile backlog with weekly releases. The product owner wants a single evolving structure, maintained continuously, that shows all desired features ranked by priority for the delivery-tracking product, without producing a one-off baselined specification document.

Which documentation structure (EU 3.6) best fits?
questions.explanation: A continuously evolving, priority-ranked collection of desired features maintained without a one-off baselined document is precisely a product backlog, one of the "alternative documentation structures" the syllabus lists alongside sprint backlogs and story maps.
questions.reference: EU3.6 — Requirements Documents and Documentation Structures

questions.prompt: Judge each statement about requirements management practices (EU 6.5, 6.8) as TRUE or FALSE.

statements.text: The set of attributes to define for requirements should depend on the information needs of the different stakeholders in the project.
Prioritization should always be based on exactly one universal assessment criterion, such as cost, regardless of the project.
Ad-hoc and analytical prioritization techniques are the two categories into which prioritization techniques can be classified.
Defining the stakeholders to be involved is one of the recommended steps before performing prioritization.

questions.explanation: Attribute sets should indeed be defined based on stakeholders' information needs (1 true). Prioritization is not limited to one universal criterion; multiple criteria such as business value, urgency, effort, and dependencies may be used depending on the chosen technique (2 false). Ad-hoc and analytical are indeed the two named categories of prioritization techniques (3 true), and defining which stakeholders must be involved is one of the recommended prioritization steps (4 true).

questions.prompt:
Before building real functionality, the ParcelPath UX team creates clickable screens of the new "live courier map" feature using a dedicated prototyping tool. Shoppers can tap around the screens and give feedback on the layout, but tapping a button does not actually fetch real courier GPS data.

What kind of prototype is this (EU 3.7)?
questions.explanation: Real screens with click flows but no real functionality, used to specify and validate the user interface, is the definition of a mock-up (medium-fidelity prototype). A wireframe is lower fidelity (simple sketches), and a native prototype implements real, working functionality.

questions.prompt: A ParcelPath requirement reads: "The system should probably show delivery progress to most users in a reasonably fast way." Stakeholders agree this is roughly what they want, but nobody can say when it would count as fulfilled. Judge each statement (EU 3.8) as TRUE or FALSE.

statements.text: This requirement is unambiguous, since all stakeholders agree on what "reasonably fast" means.
This requirement fails the verifiable quality criterion, because there is no indisputable way to check whether "reasonably fast" has been achieved.
Because the requirement is adequate and understandable, its lack of verifiability is irrelevant and can safely be ignored.
Determining whether this requirement is necessary requires checking that it contributes to at least one stakeholder goal — independent of whether it is phrased precisely.
This is a quality-criteria issue at the single-requirement level; it has no bearing on the Consistent or Traceable criteria, which apply to work products containing multiple requirements.

questions.explanation: The requirement is in fact ambiguous because "reasonably fast" is not shared/agreed, so statement 1 is false. It indeed fails verifiability since no indisputable check exists for "reasonably fast," making statement 2 true. Verifiability still matters (e.g., for acceptance), so it cannot be ignored just because other criteria are met — statement 3 is false. Necessity is assessed by whether the requirement serves a stakeholder goal, independent of its phrasing — statement 4 is true. The described defect is a single-requirement quality issue and is conceptually distinct from work-product-level criteria like consistency or traceability — statement 5 is true.
questions.reference: EU3.8 — Quality Criteria for Work Products and Requirements
